text: Six ideas follow from that, and the sections below teach each one: In Python In C++ Why C++ does it this way Section You run the source file A compiler turns each .cpp file into machine code, then a linker joins the pieces into one program Machine code runs without an interpreter, so loops cost nanoseconds, not tens of nanoseconds 1 b = a makes a second name for the same object auto b = a; makes a copy ; you ask for a reference ( & ) or a pointer ( * ) explicitly Values sit inline in memory, with no per-object header or reference count 2 Every object lives on the heap until the last reference goes Local variables live on the stack and die at the closing brace; you choose the heap when you need it The stack is free to allocate and free 3 with open(...) for cleanup RAII : every object's destructor runs at a known moment, so every resource is released by one Deterministic cleanup with no garbage collector 4 , 5 Assignment never copies a big object Move semantics : a value can hand its heap buffer to another instead of being copied Copy by default would otherwise make returning a vector expensive 6 Bugs raise exceptions Many bugs are undefined behaviour : no error, the program means nothing, and the optimiser may make it do anything Checking every index and every overflow would cost speed; C++ checks only when you ask 12 The rest (classes, templates, the standard library, lambdas, error handling) is the toolkit you write with; sections 7 to 11 teach it with the problem each feature solves, what it costs, and the usual mistakes.

text: How a C++ program is built In Python, python main.py reads your source and runs it; import tokens finds tokens.py at run time.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: C++ has no run-time import.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Building a program is a separate step with three stages, and most confusing C++ errors come from not knowing which stage complained.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Lines starting with # are text commands. #include "tokens.h" pastes the whole file in, literally.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: The result is one long file per .cpp , called a translation unit .

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Each translation unit is compiled separately into an object file ( .o ): machine code plus a table of the names ( symbols ) it defines and the ones it needs from elsewhere.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Joins the object files and libraries into one executable, matching every needed symbol to exactly one definition.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Here is the running example from the root page's Rosetta tab, cut down to its token counter and split the way real projects are: a header ( .h ) that declares the function (its name and types: a promise), and a source file that defines it (the body). tokens.h // tokens.h: the declaration (a promise that a definition exists somewhere) #pragma once #include <string_view> int count_tokens(std::string_view text); main.cpp // main.cpp: uses count_tokens; only sees the declaration #include "tokens.h" #include <cstdio> int main() { std::printf( "%d tokens\n" , count_tokens( "C++ is fun, x86_64 too" )); } tokens.cpp // tokens.cpp: the definition #include "tokens.h" #include <cctype> int count_tokens(std::string_view text) { int n = 0; bool inside = false ; for ( unsigned char c : text) { bool tok = std::isalnum(c) && c < 128; if (tok && !inside) n += 1; inside = tok; } return n; } std::string_view is a read-only view of some characters (section 9); unsigned char c : text loops over the bytes.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Stage 1, the preprocessor: how long is the translation unit the compiler actually sees for this 7-line main.cpp ?

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Predict, then reveal: how many lines does main.cpp become after #include, and what do single standard headers cost? $ wc -l main.cpp tokens.h; clang++ -std=c++20 -E main.cpp | wc -l for h in cstdio string_view vector string algorithm iostream; do printf "#include <%s> alone: " $h; printf "#include <$h>\\n" | clang++ -std=c++20 -x c++ -E - | wc -l | tr -d " "; done 7 main.cpp 4 tokens.h 11 total 55693 #include <cstdio> alone: 732 #include <string_view> alone: 55683 #include <vector> alone: 72835 #include <string> alone: 59542 #include <algorithm> alone: 54846 #include <iostream> alone: 93507 Fifty-five thousand lines, nearly all from <string_view> .

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Every .cpp that includes a standard header recompiles that header from text, which is why C++ builds are slow and why C++20 added modules (section 14) to replace textual inclusion.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Stage 2 compiles each file on its own; -c means "compile only, do not link". nm lists an object file's symbols: T is a function defined here, U is undefined here and needed from elsewhere. $ clang++ -std=c++20 -O2 -Wall -c tokens.cpp && clang++ -std=c++20 -O2 -Wall -c main.cpp && ls *.o main.o tokens.o $ nm -C main.o; echo ---; nm -C tokens.o U count_tokens(std::__1::basic_string_view<char, std::__1::char_traits<char> >) 0000000000000000 T _main U _printf 000000000000003c s l_.str 0000000000000047 s l_.str.1 0000000000000000 t ltmp0 000000000000003c s ltmp1 0000000000000060 s ltmp2 --- U __DefaultRuneLocale 0000000000000000 T count_tokens(std::__1::basic_string_view<char, std::__1::char_traits<char> >) U ___maskrune 0000000000000000 t ltmp0 00000000000000a8 s ltmp1 main.o needs count_tokens (U) and tokens.o provides it (T).

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: The compiler accepted main.cpp on the header's promise alone.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Stage 3 is the linker's job, and if you forget to give it the definition, the error comes from the linker ( ld ), not the compiler: $ clang++ main.o -o app Undefined symbols for architecture arm64: "count_tokens(std::__1::basic_string_view<char, std::__1::char_traits<char>>)", referenced from: _main in main.o ld: symbol(s) not found for architecture arm64 clang++: error: linker command failed with exit code 1 (use -v to see invocation) [exit code 1] $ clang++ main.o tokens.o -o app && ./app 6 tokens The other classic link error is the opposite: two definitions.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: C++'s one definition rule (ODR) says a function may be defined once in the whole program.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Put a function body in a header, include the header from two .cpp files, and each object file gets its own copy: util.h #pragma once // A function DEFINED in a header, not marked inline int twice( int x) { return 2 * x; } b.cpp #include "util.h" int a(); int main() { return a() + twice(2) - 6; } $ clang++ -std=c++20 -c a.cpp b.cpp && clang++ a.o b.o -o app duplicate symbol 'twice(int)' in: odr/a.o odr/b.o ld: 1 duplicate symbols clang++: error: linker command failed with exit code 1 (use -v to see invocation) [exit code 1] The fix is the keyword inline , which tells the linker "identical copies of this may appear in several object files; keep one".

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Functions defined inside a class body, templates and constexpr functions are implicitly inline, which is why headers full of them link fine. util_inline.h #pragma once // The fix: inline allows one identical definition per translation unit inline int twice( int x) { return 2 * x; } $ sed -i.bak "s/util.h/util_inline.h/" a.cpp b.cpp && clang++ -std=c++20 -c a.cpp b.cpp && clang++ a.o b.o -o app && ./app; echo "exit code $?" exit code 0 Python bridge A header is like a .pyi stub (types only) that every user pastes into their file.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Python resolves names when the line runs; C++ resolves them at link time, so a missing or duplicated function is a build error, never a run-time NameError .

text: CMake: the build system Typing compiler commands does not scale past a few files.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: CMake is the de facto standard build description: you list targets (executables, libraries) and their properties, and CMake generates the commands for a fast build tool such as Ninja.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Three lines make a project: CMakeLists.txt cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.28) project(hello LANGUAGES CXX) add_executable(hello main.cpp) $ cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ > /dev/null && cmake --build build && ./build/hello [1/2] Building CXX object CMakeFiles/hello.dir/main.cpp.o [2/2] Linking CXX executable hello hello from CMake A real project separates a library from the program that uses it.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: PUBLIC properties travel to every target that links the library; PRIVATE ones do not.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: This is the single most useful idea in CMake: CMakeLists.txt cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.28) project(tokcount LANGUAGES CXX) # A library target: compiled once, linked into anything that needs it add_library(tokens src/tokens.cpp) target_include_directories(tokens PUBLIC src) # users of tokens see src/ target_compile_features(tokens PUBLIC cxx_std_20) # and get C++20 target_compile_options(tokens PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra) add_executable(tokcount src/main.cpp) target_link_libraries(tokcount PRIVATE tokens) # brings the include dir and C++20 along $ cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja && cmake --build build --verbose clang++ -Icmake2/src -std=gnu++20 -arch arm64 -o CMakeFiles/tokcount.dir/src/main.cpp.o -c cmake2/src/main.cpp clang++ -Icmake2/src -std=gnu++20 -arch arm64 -Wall -Wextra -o CMakeFiles/tokens.dir/src/tokens.cpp.o -c cmake2/src/tokens.cpp cmake -E rm -f libtokens.a && ar qc libtokens.a CMakeFiles/tokens.dir/src/tokens.cpp.o && ranlib libtokens.a && cmake -E touch libtokens.a clang++ -arch arm64 -Wl,-search_paths_first -Wl,-headerpad_max_install_names CMakeFiles/tokcount.dir/src/main.cpp.o -o tokcount libtokens.a $ ./build/tokcount 6 tokens Read the generated commands: -Icmake2/src and -std=gnu++20 reached main.cpp because they are PUBLIC on tokens ; -Wall -Wextra did not, because it is PRIVATE .

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: The library became a static library libtokens.a (an archive of object files, made by ar ) and was copied into the executable at link time.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: The payoff of separate compilation is incremental builds: editing a .cpp recompiles one file, editing a header recompiles everything that includes it. $ touch src/tokens.cpp && cmake --build build [1/3] Building CXX object CMakeFiles/tokens.dir/src/tokens.cpp.o [2/3] Linking CXX static library libtokens.a [3/3] Linking CXX executable tokcount $ touch src/tokens.h && cmake --build build [1/4] Building CXX object CMakeFiles/tokcount.dir/src/main.cpp.o [2/4] Building CXX object CMakeFiles/tokens.dir/src/tokens.cpp.o [3/4] Linking CXX static library libtokens.a [4/4] Linking CXX executable tokcount $ cmake --build build ninja: no work to do.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: Problem it solves Compile each file once, in parallel, and rebuild only what changed.

section: 1. how a c++ program is built
text: What it costs Headers are re-parsed in every file that includes them; you maintain declarations and definitions separately.

Values, references and pointers In Python every variable is a name bound to an object somewhere on the heap, and b = a binds a second name to the same object.
In C++ a variable is the object: its bytes live where the variable lives.
So assignment and initialisation copy , and if you want a second name you must say so.
There are two ways: A reference , T& r = a; , is another name for an existing object.
It must be bound when created and can never be re-bound or be null.
Using it is exactly like using a .
A pointer , T* p = &a; , is a variable holding an address. &a means "the address of a"; *p means "the object at p"; p->f() is short for (*p).f() .

A pointer can be re-pointed, and can be nullptr (points at nothing). copy.cpp #include <cstdio> #include <vector> int main() { std::vector< int > a{1, 2, 3}; std::vector< int > b = a; // a COPY: b gets its own three ints b.push_back(4); std::printf( "a has %zu, b has %zu
" , a.size(), b.size()); std::vector< int >& r = a; // a REFERENCE: another name for a r.push_back(99); std::printf( "a has %zu after r.push_back
" , a.size()); std::vector< int >* p = &a; // a POINTER: holds a's address p->push_back(7); // -> follows the pointer std::printf( "a has %zu after p->push_back; p == &a is %d
" , a.size(), p == &a); p = nullptr ; // a pointer can be re-pointed, or point at nothing std::printf( "p is now %s
" , p ? "set" : "null" ); } Predict, then reveal: what sizes does each line print? $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra copy.cpp -o copy && ./copy a has 3, b has 4 a has 4 after r.push_back a has 5 after p->push_back; p == &a is 1 p is now null copy.py a = [1, 2, 3] b = a # no copy: a second name for the same list b.append(4) print(f "a has {len(a)}, b has {len(b)}" ) $ python3.14 copy.py a has 4, b has 4 The same three lines in Python give "a has 4, b has 4": one list, two names.
C++ printed "a has 3, b has 4": two vectors.
Neither reference nor pointer keeps a alive; they only refer to memory that a owns.
That is the root of every dangling-reference bug (section 12). const const marks something read-only, checked by the compiler.
The most common use is the parameter type const T& : "let me read your object without copying it, and I promise not to change it".

[exit code 1] Three errors, all at compile time.
The second one shows a feature of C++ error messages you will meet constantly: the compiler lists every overload of += it tried and why each failed ("method is not marked const").
Read the first line and the line pointing at your own file; skim the candidates.
Pass by T for small values (int, double, a pointer, a string_view ); const T& to read a big object; T& to modify the caller's object; T* when "no object" is a valid answer.
What it costs Copies are real: passing a std::vector by value copies every element.
Common mistakes Passing big objects by value by accident; a reference or pointer that outlives its object.
The stack and the heap A C++ object lives in one of three kinds of storage, and the kind decides when it dies: Automatic storage, "the stack".
Each function call pushes a frame of memory for its locals; the frame is popped when the function returns.
Allocation is free (the stack pointer moves) and destruction happens at the closing brace } , in reverse order of creation.
Dynamic storage, "the heap".
Objects created with new (or, properly, std::make_unique , section 5).
They live until someone destroys them.
Allocation calls the memory allocator ( malloc ), which costs tens of nanoseconds and can fragment memory.
Globals and static variables: they live for the whole program.
Python puts every object on the heap and frees it when its reference count reaches zero.
C++ lets you put most things on the stack.

Printing the addresses shows the three regions (the exact numbers change on every run, because macOS randomises where each region starts): stack_heap.cpp #include <cstdio> #include <memory> #include <vector> int global_counter = 0; // static storage: lives for the whole program void show( const char * what, const void * p) { std::printf( "%-28s %p\n" , what, p); } int main() { int on_stack = 1; // automatic storage (the stack) int also_on_stack = 2; auto on_heap = std::make_unique< int >(3); // dynamic storage (the heap) std::vector< int > v{1, 2, 3}; // the vector object is on the stack... show( "&global_counter (static)" , &global_counter); show( "&on_stack" , &on_stack); show( "&also_on_stack" , &also_on_stack); show( "&v (the vector object)" , &v); show( "on_heap.get() (heap int)" , on_heap.get()); show( "v.data() (its elements)" , v.data()); // ...its elements are on the heap std::printf( "sizeof(v) = %zu bytes, whatever v.size() is\n" , sizeof (v)); } $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra stack_heap.cpp -o stack_heap && ./stack_heap &global_counter (static) 0x1021cc000 &on_stack 0x16dc3a73c &also_on_stack 0x16dc3a738 &v (the vector object) 0x16dc3a720 on_heap.get() (heap int) 0x1028253f0 v.data() (its elements) 0x102825400 sizeof(v) = 24 bytes, whatever v.size() is The stack addresses ( 0x16... ) go down as variables are added: on this ARM Mac the stack grows towards lower addresses.

The vector is a hybrid that you will meet everywhere: the std::vector object itself is 24 bytes on the stack (a pointer to the elements, the size, the capacity), and its elements live in a heap buffer it owns.
When the vector dies, its destructor frees the buffer.
That pattern, a small owner on the stack and a big buffer on the heap, is how C++ gets automatic cleanup of heap memory.
It has a name: RAII.

Go deeper: why stack memory is fast (it is almost always in the CPU cache) and what the heap allocator does are Part 2 's subject; the root's Reading section 5 draws the same records laid out in Python, C++ and Rust.

RAII and destructors A class can define a constructor (runs when an object is created) and a destructor , written ~ClassName() , which runs automatically when the object dies: at the closing brace for a local, when its owner dies for a member, when delete is called for a heap object.

RAII ("resource acquisition is initialisation", an awkward name for a simple idea) means: tie every resource (memory, a file, a lock, a GPU buffer, a socket) to an object whose destructor releases it.
Then you can never forget to release it, even when an exception jumps out of the function.

To see it happen, this page uses a small class, Tracer , that prints a line from each special member function, numbering objects #1 , #2 ... and saying whether each lives on the stack or the heap (its source is in the Object lifetimes tab).

First, scopes: lifetime.cpp (lines 14 to 22) void scope() { Tracer a{ "a" }; { Tracer b{ "b" }; STEP( "end of inner block" ); } Tracer c{ "c" }; STEP( "end of function" ); } Predict, then reveal: in what order are a, b and c destroyed? $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra lifetime.cpp -o lifetime && ./lifetime scope ctor #1 a stack L15 ctor #2 b stack L17 @18 end of inner block dtor #2 ctor #3 c stack L20 @21 end of function dtor #3 dtor #1 @0 back in main b dies at its inner brace, before c is even created; at the end, c dies before a: reverse order of construction, always.

(Lines starting with @ are the program's own STEP markers, with their line numbers.) Now an exception: lifetime.cpp (lines 94 to 104) void unwind() { Tracer a{ "a" }; try { Tracer b{ "b" }; throw std::runtime_error( "boom" ); STEP( "never reached" ); } catch ( const std::exception& e) { std::printf( "caught %s\n" , e.what()); } STEP( "end of function" ); } Predict, then reveal: which destructors run, and when, relative to "caught boom"? $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra lifetime.cpp -o lifetime && ./lifetime unwind ctor #1 a stack L95 ctor #2 b stack L97 dtor #2 caught boom @103 end of function dtor #1 @0 back in main When throw leaves the try block, C++ unwinds the stack : it destroys every local in the scopes being left (b) before the catch runs.
This is why RAII and exceptions work together, and why C++ code almost never needs finally .
Python bridge with open(p) as f: is RAII you opt into for one block.
In C++ every object behaves like a with block, and the "exit" is the destructor.
Python's __del__ is not the equivalent: it runs whenever the reference count or the garbage collector gets to it.
Problem it solves Leaks and forgotten cleanup, including on error paths.
What it costs Nothing at run time beyond the destructor's own work.
Common mistakes Holding a resource in a raw pointer instead of an owning object; a destructor that throws (it must not: a second exception during unwinding terminates the program).

[exit code 1] Sizes, measured ( sizeof gives an object's size in bytes): $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra sizes.cpp -o sizes && ./sizes int* 8 std::unique_ptr<int> 8 std::shared_ptr<int> 16 std::vector<int> 24 std::string 24 std::string_view 16 std::span<int> 16 std::optional<int> 8 std::function<int(int)> 32 Plain {double; f()} 8 Virtual {double; virtual f()} 16 Rule unique_ptr by default; shared_ptr only when ownership is genuinely shared (a cache entry used by several requests); raw pointers and references only to observe an object someone else owns.

text: Rust bridge If you go on to the Rust page : Box<T> is unique_ptr , Rc<T> / Arc<T> are shared_ptr without and with atomic counts, and Rust's compiler enforces the "do not use after move" rule that C++ only recommends.
Move semantics Copy-by-default has an obvious cost: returning a vector of a million elements, or putting a string into a container, would copy every byte.
C++11 added moves : when the source object is about to die anyway, the new object may steal its heap buffer (copy three pointers, set the source's to null) instead of copying the contents.
The compiler needs to know when stealing is safe.
It sorts expressions into two families (simplified): an lvalue has a name and an address you can take: a , v[3] , *p .
It will be used again, so it must be copied. an rvalue is a temporary about to disappear: make_name() , a + b , Tracer{"x"} .
It may be moved from.

A class gets a move constructor T(T&& other) (the && means "rvalue reference": binds only to things that may be moved from) alongside its copy constructor T(const T& other) , and overload resolution picks one. std::move(x) moves nothing.

It is a cast that says "treat x as an rvalue; I will not need its value again" ( cppreference: "exactly equivalent to a static_cast to an rvalue reference type" ); the move constructor that it selects does the stealing. lifetime.cpp (lines 26 to 33) void copymove() { Tracer a{ "a" }; Tracer b = a; // copy constructor Tracer c = std::move(a); // move constructor: steals a's string std::printf( "a.name is now \"%s\"\n" , a.name.c_str()); b = c; // copy assignment (b already exists) STEP( "end of function" ); } Predict, then reveal: which constructors run, and what is left in a.name? $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra lifetime.cpp -o lifetime && ./lifetime copymove ctor #1 a stack L27 copy #2 from #1 a stack L28 move #3 from #1 a stack L29 a.name is now "" copy= #2 from #3 @32 end of function dtor #3 dtor #2 dtor #1 @0 back in main The moved-from a is still a valid object (its destructor runs, #1, at the end) but its value is unspecified; libc++ leaves the string empty.
You may assign to it or destroy it; do not read it.

What moving buys, and one trap: moved_from.cpp #include <cstdio> #include <string> #include <utility> #include <vector> int main() { std::string s = "a string long enough to live on the heap" ; std::string t = std::move(s); // t steals s's heap buffer std::printf( "t: %zu chars, s: %zu chars
" , t.size(), s.size()); s = "reusable" ; // a moved-from object can be assigned to std::printf( "s: %s
" , s.c_str()); std::vector< int > v(1 '000' 000, 7); const int * before = v.data(); std::vector< int > w = std::move(v); // O(1): three pointers change hands std::printf( "w.data() == old v.data(): %d, v.size() now %zu
" , w.data() == before, v.size()); const std::string c = "const" ; std::string d = std::move(c); // compiles, but COPIES: you cannot steal from const std::printf( "c after 'move': %s
" , c.c_str()); } $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra moved_from.cpp -o moved_from && ./moved_from t: 40 chars, s: 0 chars s: reusable w.data() == old v.data(): 1, v.size() now 0 c after 'move': const The million-element vector changed hands in constant time: w owns the very same buffer.
The last line is the trap: std::move of a const object silently copies, because a move constructor needs to modify its source.
When the compiler copies, moves or does neither Passing and returning values is where moves matter most.

One rule removes most of the worry: since C++17, returning a temporary, and in practice a local variable, constructs the result directly in the caller's variable, with no copy and no move ( copy elision , cppreference ).

So return big objects by value; never write return std::move(local); , which can only prevent elision. lifetime.cpp (lines 8 to 10) void by_value(Tracer) { STEP( "inside by_value" ); } void by_ref( const Tracer&) { STEP( "inside by_ref" ); } Tracer make( const char * n) { Tracer t{n}; return t; } lifetime.cpp (lines 37 to 44) void calls() { Tracer a{ "a" }; by_ref(a); // no new object by_value(a); // a copy for the parameter by_value(std::move(a)); // a move for the parameter Tracer m = make( "m" ); // no copy, no move: built in place STEP( "end of function" ); } Predict, then reveal: how many Tracer objects get made in total, and where does m come from? $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra lifetime.cpp -o lifetime && ./lifetime calls ctor #1 a stack L38 @9 inside by_ref copy #2 from #1 a stack L40 @8 inside by_value dtor #2 move #3 from #1 a stack L41 @8 inside by_value dtor #3 ctor #4 m stack L10 @43 end of function dtor #4 dtor #1 @0 back in main Why noexcept on a move constructor matters: one vector, two classes A std::vector keeps its elements in one buffer.
When the buffer is full, push_back allocates a bigger one, transfers the old elements and frees the old buffer.
It would like to move them, but if a move threw an exception halfway, the old buffer would be half-emptied and the vector could not restore it.
So the standard library moves only if the move constructor is declared noexcept ("this never throws"); otherwise it copies, to keep its strong exception guarantee ( std::move_if_noexcept ).
The animation runs the same three push_back calls on two versions of Tracer that differ only in that one keyword.
Everything shown is the program's real output.

Move is noexcept Move without noexcept (before) With noexcept , each reallocation moves (cheap); without it, the same code copies every existing element on every growth: for a vector of strings, that is a heap allocation and a byte copy per element.
The compiler writes a noexcept move constructor for you when every member's is noexcept (the rule of zero, below), which is one more reason not to write them by hand.
The rule of zero and the rule of five Five special member functions control a class's lifetime: destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment.
The compiler writes all five for you, member by member.
That is correct when every member manages itself ( std::vector , std::string , std::unique_ptr ): the rule of zero says write none of them.

A class that owns a raw resource must write all five (the rule of five ), because the compiler-written copy would copy the pointer, not the buffer: rule_of_five.cpp (lines 5 to 35) // A class that owns a raw buffer must write all five special members. class Buffer { float * data_; std::size_t n_; public : explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : data_( new float [n]()), n_(n) {} ~Buffer() { delete [] data_; } // 1 destructor Buffer( const Buffer& o) : data_( new float [o.n_]), n_(o.n_) { // 2 copy constructor std::memcpy(data_, o.data_, n_ * sizeof ( float )); } Buffer& operator =( const Buffer& o) { // 3 copy assignment Buffer tmp(o); swap(tmp); return * this ; } Buffer(Buffer&& o) noexcept // 4 move constructor : data_(std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr )), n_(std::exchange(o.n_, 0)) {} Buffer& operator =(Buffer&& o) noexcept { // 5 move assignment Buffer tmp(std::move(o)); swap(tmp); return * this ; } void swap(Buffer& o) noexcept { std::swap(data_, o.data_); std::swap(n_, o.n_); } std::size_t size() const { return n_; } }; // Rule of zero: let a member that already manages itself do the work. #include <vector> struct Buffer0 { std::vector< float > data; // the compiler writes all five, correctly }; $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra rule_of_five.cpp -o rule_of_five && ./rule_of_five b 4, c 4, moved-from a 0; y 4, z 4, moved-from x 0 Thirty lines of careful code against one line ( std::vector<float> data; ).

Write only a destructor and forget the other four, and copying the object gives two owners of one buffer, freed twice: the UB gallery 's "double free" case shows the crash, and shows the bug vanishing at -O2 , where the compiler removed the allocation altogether.
Problem it solves Copy-by-default without paying for copies of temporaries and returned values.
What it costs The rules (value categories, noexcept , moved-from states) are the hardest part of the language to learn.
Common mistakes Using an object after std::move ; return std::move(x) ; a hand-written move constructor without noexcept ; moving from const .

text: Classes, operators, inheritance and virtual functions A class and a struct are the same thing except for the default: struct members are public, class members private.

section: 7. classes, operators, inheritance and virtual functions
text: Python's conventions become rules the compiler checks: private really is private, const methods really cannot modify the object, and members must be declared with their types. classes.cpp #include <compare> #include <cstdio> #include <string> class Usage { public : // explicit: no silent conversion from a string to a Usage explicit Usage(std::string user, long tokens = 0) : user_(std::move(user)), tokens_(tokens) {} // member initialiser list const std::string& user() const { return user_; } // const: does not modify *this long tokens() const { return tokens_; } Usage& operator +=( long n) { tokens_ += n; return * this ; } // one line gives ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= comparing members in declaration order auto operator <=>( const Usage&) const = default ; private : std::string user_; long tokens_; }; Usage operator +(Usage u, long n) { u += n; return u; } int main() { Usage a{ "u0005" , 4816}; Usage b = a + 100; b += 1; std::printf( "%s %ld\n" , b.user().c_str(), b.tokens()); std::printf( "a < b: %d, a == a: %d\n" , a < b, a == a); } $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra classes.cpp -o classes && ./classes u0005 4917 a < b: 1, a == a: 1 Member initialiser list ( : user_(...), tokens_(...) ): members are constructed there, before the body runs, in the order they are declared in the class (not the order you list them; clang warns when they differ). explicit forbids using the constructor as a silent conversion.

bool in = false ; for ( char c : s) { bool t = c != ' ' ; n += t && !in; in = t; } return n; } }; struct Bytes : Tokenizer { int count( const std::string& s) const override { return static_cast < int >(s.size()); } }; int main() { std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Tokenizer>> ts; ts.push_back(std::make_unique<Whitespace>()); ts.push_back(std::make_unique<Bytes>()); for ( const auto & t : ts) // which count() runs is decided at run time std::printf( "%d\n" , t->count( "hello token world" )); } $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra virtual.cpp -o virtual && ./virtual 3 17 What a virtual call costs here: the same sum over 10 million objects, called three ways (best of 7 runs, the laptop's load average printed first): vcost.cpp (lines 7 to 9) struct Shape { virtual long area() const = 0; virtual ~Shape() = default ; }; struct Sq : Shape { long s; explicit Sq( long v) : s(v) {} long area() const override { return s * s; } }; struct SqPlain { long s; long area() const { return s * s; } }; // no virtual vcost.cpp (lines 24 to 35) std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> virt; // (a) heap objects, virtual call std::vector<std::unique_ptr<SqPlain>> boxed; // (b) heap objects, ordinary call std::vector<SqPlain> flat; // (c) contiguous values, ordinary call for ( int i = 0; i < N; ++i) { virt.push_back(std::make_unique<Sq>(i % 7)); boxed.push_back(std::make_unique<SqPlain>(SqPlain{i % 7})); flat.push_back({i % 7}); } volatile long sink; double a = best_ms([&] { long s = 0; for ( auto & p : virt) s += p->area(); sink = s; }); double b = best_ms([&] { long s = 0; for ( auto & p : boxed) s += p->area(); sink = s; }); double c = best_ms([&] { long s = 0; for ( auto & q : flat) s += q.area(); sink = s; }); $ sysctl -n vm.loadavg; clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 vcost.cpp -o vcost && ./vcost { 13.10 8.35 7.33 } (a) virtual call, objects behind pointers: 1.01 ns per object (b) ordinary call, objects behind pointers: 0.47 ns per object (c) ordinary call, objects in a flat vector: 0.34 ns per object The virtual call itself (a vs b) roughly doubled the time per object, mostly because the compiler cannot inline a call it cannot predict; Templates and concepts Python functions accept anything with the right methods (duck typing), checked when the line runs.
A C++ template is a pattern from which the compiler writes a separate function or class for each type you use it with ( instantiation , or monomorphisation), checked at compile time.

The generated code is as fast as if you had written each version by hand: no boxing, no dispatch. templates.cpp #include <cstdio> #include <string> #include <vector> // One template, many functions: the compiler writes a copy per type used. template < typename T> T total( const std::vector<T>& xs) { T sum{}; for ( const T& x : xs) sum += x; return sum; } template < typename K, typename V> struct Pair { K key; V value; }; // a class template int main() { std::printf( "%d
" , total(std::vector< int >{1, 2, 3})); std::printf( "%.1f
" , total(std::vector< double >{0.5, 0.25})); std::printf( "%s
" , total(std::vector<std::string>{ "to" , "ken" }).c_str()); Pair<std::string, long > p{ "u0029" , 9491}; std::printf( "%s %ld
" , p.key.c_str(), p.value); } $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra templates.cpp -o templates && ./templates 6 0.8 token u0029 9491 One template, three real functions in the object file: $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O0 -c templates.cpp -o templates.o && nm -C templates.o | grep " total<" 0000000000000580 T std::__1::basic_string<char, std::__1::char_traits<char>, std::__1::allocator<char> > total<std::__1::basic_string<char, std::__1::char_traits<char>, std::__1::allocator<char> > >(std::__1::vector<std::__1::basic_string<char, std::__1::char_traits<char>, std::__1::allocator<char> >, std::__1::allocator<std::__1::basic_string<char, std::__1::char_traits<char>, std::__1::allocator<char> > > > const&) 0000000000000488 T double total<double>(std::__1::vector<double, std::__1::allocator<double> > const&) 0000000000000394 T int total<int>(std::__1::vector<int, std::__1::allocator<int> > const&) The cost shows up when the type does not fit.
Without constraints, the error appears deep inside the template body, at the line that failed, and the compiler explains the whole chain of instantiations that led there.
For a small template that is readable; for a standard algorithm it is not.

Here is std::sort on a struct with no < , against C++20's std::ranges::sort , which states its requirements as concepts : $ for f in sort_err rsort_err; do printf "%-10s %4s lines of diagnostics, %s errors\n" $f $(clang++ -std=c++23 -c $f.cpp -o /dev/null 2>&1 | wc -l) $(clang++ -std=c++23 -c $f.cpp -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -c " error: "); done sort_err 308 lines of diagnostics, 20 errors rsort_err 34 lines of diagnostics, 1 errors A concept is a named, compile-time predicate on types.

Using it in a template's signature makes the compiler check it at the call, and the error names the requirement that failed: concept_err.cpp #include <vector> // A concept names the requirement: T must support += and start from T{} template < typename T> concept Summable = requires (T a, T b) { T{}; a += b; }; template <Summable T> T total( const std::vector<T>& xs) { T sum{}; for ( const T& x : xs) sum += x; return sum; } struct Msg { const char * text; }; int main() { std::vector<Msg> msgs{{ "hi" }, { "there" }}; total(msgs); // rejected at the call, with the reason } $ clang++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -c concept_err.cpp -o /dev/null concept_err.cpp:16:5: error: no matching function for call to 'total' 16 | total(msgs); // rejected at the call, with the reason | ^~~~~ concept_err.cpp:7:3: note: candidate template ignored: constraints not satisfied [with T = Msg] 7 | T total(const std::vector<T>& xs) { | ^ concept_err.cpp:6:11: note: because 'Msg' does not satisfy 'Summable' 6 | template <Summable T> | ^ concept_err.cpp:4:48: note: because 'a += b' would be invalid: no viable overloaded '+=' 4 | concept Summable = requires(T a, T b) { T{}; a += b; }; | ^ 1 error generated. [exit code 1] Python bridge A concept is like a typing.Protocol that the compiler enforces at every call, and a template is like a generic function where the type checker is the compiler.
The difference: Python runs one function for all types; C++ compiles one per type, which costs compile time and binary size.
Problem it solves Generic code at full speed (the standard library is almost all templates).
What it costs Compile time, binary size, and template code must live in headers (the compiler needs the body to instantiate it).
Common mistakes Unconstrained templates with unreadable errors; heavy template metaprogramming where a plain function would do.

text: Common mistakes Keeping a reference or iterator across a push_back ; map[key] to test membership; std::list (a linked list, almost always slower than vector ).
Lambdas A lambda is an inline function, like Python's lambda but with statements allowed.

The part in square brackets says which outside variables it captures and how: [x] copies x when the lambda is created; [&x] refers to the variable itself; [=] and [&] capture everything used, by copy or by reference. lambdas.cpp #include <cstdio> #include <functional> #include <vector> int main() { int threshold = 10; auto by_value = [threshold]( int n) { return n > threshold; }; // copies threshold now auto by_ref = [&threshold]( int n) { return n > threshold; }; // refers to the variable threshold = 100; std::printf( "by_value(50)=%d by_ref(50)=%d
" , by_value(50), by_ref(50)); int calls = 0; auto counter = [calls]() mutable { return ++calls; }; // mutable: may change its own copy counter(); counter(); std::printf( "counter() -> %d, outer calls still %d
" , counter(), calls); auto twice = []( auto x) { return x + x; }; // generic lambda (a template) std::printf( "twice(21)=%d twice(1.5)=%.1f
" , twice(21), twice(1.5)); // A lambda is an object of a compiler-written class; its size is its captures std::printf( "sizeof: no capture %zu, one int %zu, one reference %zu
" , sizeof ([] {}), sizeof (by_value), sizeof (by_ref)); std::function< bool ( int )> f = by_value; // type-erased holder: can store any callable std::printf( "sizeof(std::function) %zu
" , sizeof (f)); } Predict, then reveal: by_value(50) and by_ref(50) after threshold becomes 100? $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra lambdas.cpp -o lambdas && ./lambdas by_value(50)=1 by_ref(50)=0 counter() -> 3, outer calls still 0 twice(21)=42 twice(1.5)=3.0 sizeof: no capture 1, one int 4, one reference 8 sizeof(std::function) 32 Under the hood a lambda is an object of a class the compiler writes, with the captures as members and operator() as the body; its size is the size of its captures.

Python closures always capture variables by reference and keep them alive; a C++ reference capture does not keep anything alive, so a lambda that outlives the function it was made in (returned, stored, or given to a thread) must capture by value. std::function can hold any callable with a given signature, at the price of a type-erased call and possibly a heap allocation; templates and auto parameters avoid both.
Problem it solves Comparators, callbacks and small helpers written where they are used.
What it costs Nothing for a lambda passed to a template; a std::function costs an indirect call.
Common mistakes [&] in a lambda that escapes its scope (the gallery's "dangling capture" case); capturing this and outliving the object.

Error handling: exceptions, optional, expected C++ has three ways to say "this did not work", and real code uses all three: errors.cpp #include <charconv> #include <cstdio> #include <expected> #include <optional> #include <stdexcept> #include <string> #include <string_view> // 1.

Exceptions: like Python's raise/except long parse_or_throw(std::string_view s) { long v = 0; auto [p, ec] = std::from_chars(s.data(), s.data() + s.size(), v); if (ec != std::errc{} || p != s.data() + s.size()) throw std::invalid_argument( "not a number: " + std::string(s)); return v; } // 2. optional: "a value or nothing", no reason given (like returning None) std::optional< long > parse_opt(std::string_view s) { long v = 0; auto [p, ec] = std::from_chars(s.data(), s.data() + s.size(), v); if (ec != std::errc{} || p != s.data() + s.size()) return std::nullopt; return v; } // 3. expected (C++23): "a value or an error", like Rust's Result enum class ParseError { empty, not_a_number }; std::expected< long , ParseError> parse_exp(std::string_view s) { if (s.empty()) return std::unexpected(ParseError::empty); long v = 0; auto [p, ec] = std::from_chars(s.data(), s.data() + s.size(), v); if (ec != std::errc{} || p != s.data() + s.size()) return std::unexpected(ParseError::not_a_number); return v; } int main() { try { parse_or_throw( "12x" ); } catch ( const std::invalid_argument& e) { std::printf( "caught: %s
" , e.what()); } auto o = parse_opt( "12x" ); std::printf( "optional: has_value=%d, value_or(-1)=%ld
" , o.has_value(), o.value_or(-1)); for (std::string_view s : { "4816" , "" , "12x" }) { auto r = parse_exp(s) .transform([]( long v) { return v * 2; }); // runs only on success if (r) std::printf( "expected "%.*s": value %ld
" , ( int )s.size(), s.data(), *r); else std::printf( "expected "%.*s": error %d
" , ( int )s.size(), s.data(), ( int )r.error()); } } $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra errors.cpp -o errors && ./errors caught: not a number: 12x optional: has_value=0, value_or(-1)=-1 expected "4816": value 9632 expected "": error 0 expected "12x": error 1 Exceptions work like Python's: throw , try / catch , unwinding with destructors (section 4).

Use them for errors the immediate caller cannot handle (a missing config file, out of memory). std::optional<T> (C++17) is "a T or nothing", like returning None , with no reason attached. std::expected<T, E> (C++23) is "a T or an error E", like Rust's Result .
The caller must look; transform and and_then chain steps that run only on success.
Use it for failures that are part of normal operation (parsing user input, a malformed JSONL line).

What each costs, measured with the same tiny function written both ways (10 million successful calls; 100,000 failing calls): $ sysctl -n vm.loadavg; clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 throw_cost.cpp -o throw_cost && ./throw_cost { 13.33 8.47 7.38 } success path: exception-style 1.51 ns/call, expected-style 0.98 ns/call failure path: throw+catch 4766 ns/call, expected 0.96 ns/call On the success path both are about a nanosecond: compilers implement exceptions with tables consulted only when something is thrown ("zero-cost" exceptions, which still cost binary size).
Throwing and catching took about 4766 ns, thousands of times more than returning an expected .
So: exceptions for rare failures, expected or optional where failure is common.

Some codebases (game engines, parts of Google's, many embedded ones) compile with exceptions turned off; ggml, the C core under llama.cpp, reports errors with return values and assertions, since C has no exceptions.
Rule of thumb Exceptional and far away: throw.
Expected and handled by the caller: std::expected . "Not found": std::optional . noexcept Mark functions that never throw, above all move constructors and destructors (section 6).
Common mistakes Exceptions as control flow in a hot loop; throwing from a destructor; ignoring an expected (add [[nodiscard]] to the function).

Undefined behaviour The C++ standard lists operations whose result it does not define: reading outside an array, reading freed memory, overflowing a signed integer, reading an uninitialised variable, two threads writing the same variable without synchronisation, falling off the end of a function that should return a value, and others.
Such a program has undefined behaviour (UB): not "a wrong answer" but no meaning at all.
The compiler is allowed to assume UB never happens , and its optimiser uses that assumption to delete checks and simplify code.
So a program with UB can work at -O0 and break at -O2 , or work today and break after a compiler upgrade.
This is the deepest difference from Python, where every one of these is either impossible or an exception.

The classic example: "will x + 1 overflow?" written the obvious way. overflow.cpp #include <climits> #include <cstdio> // "Will adding 1 overflow?" written the way you would in Python __attribute__((noinline)) bool will_overflow( int x) { return x + 1 < x; // signed overflow is UB, so the compiler may assume x + 1 > x } int main() { std::printf( "will_overflow(INT_MAX) = %d\n" , will_overflow(INT_MAX)); } $ clang++-23 -std=c++23 -O0 overflow.cpp -o overflow && ./overflow will_overflow(INT_MAX) = 1 $ clang++-23 -std=c++23 -O2 overflow.cpp -o overflow && ./overflow will_overflow(INT_MAX) = 0 At -O0 the addition wrapped around to a negative number and the test said 1.
At -O2 the compiler reasoned "signed overflow cannot happen, so x + 1 < x is always false" and compiled the function to return false .
Neither build reported anything.

Sanitizers are compiler modes that add run-time checks for UB; UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan) catches this one: $ clang++-23 -std=c++23 -O2 -fsanitize=undefined overflow.cpp -o overflow && ./overflow overflow.cpp:6:14: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int' SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior overflow.cpp:6:14 will_overflow(INT_MAX) = 1 (Under UBSan the program prints 1 again: the instrumented build computes the addition so it can check it.) The fix is to test before adding: x == INT_MAX , or __builtin_add_overflow , or C++26's <stdckdint.h> checked arithmetic.
Unsigned integers do not have this problem: they wrap around by definition.

A second one, the uninitialised variable, shows how odd UB can look. seen is never set when flag is false: uninit.cpp #include <cstdio> __attribute__((noinline)) void report( bool flag) { bool seen; // never initialised when flag is false if (flag) seen = true ; if (seen) std::printf( "seen
" ); if (!seen) std::printf( "not seen
" ); std::printf( "done
" ); } int main() { report( false ); } $ clang++-23 -std=c++23 -O0 uninit.cpp -o uninit && ./uninit not seen done $ clang++-23 -std=c++23 -O2 uninit.cpp -o uninit && ./uninit seen done The same call printed "not seen" at -O0 and "seen" at -O2 .

The compiler warned, though only with -Wall : $ clang++-23 -std=c++23 -Wall -c uninit.cpp -o /dev/null uninit.cpp:5:9: warning: variable 'seen' is used uninitialized whenever 'if' condition is false [-Wsometimes-uninitialized] 5 | if (flag) seen = true; | ^~~~ uninit.cpp:6:9: note: uninitialized use occurs here 6 | if (seen) std::printf("seen\n"); | ^~~~ uninit.cpp:5:5: note: remove the 'if' if its condition is always true 5 | if (flag) seen = true; | ^~~~~~~~~ uninit.cpp:4:14: note: initialize the variable 'seen' to silence this warning 4 | bool seen; // never initialised when flag is false | ^ | = false 1 warning generated.

The UB gallery tab has ten cases (overflow, uninitialised read, out-of-bounds index, off-by-one loop, reference into a reallocated vector, string_view of a temporary, dangling lambda capture, double free, missing return, data race), each with its -O0 run, -O2 run and the tool that catches it.
Your defences Warnings : -Wall -Wextra always; -Werror in CI.
They caught the uninitialised read, the dangling string_view and the missing return above.
Sanitizers in tests : -fsanitize=address (ASan: out of bounds, use after free, double free), -fsanitize=undefined (UBSan: overflow, bad shifts, missing return), -fsanitize=thread (TSan: data races).
They slow the program down (about 2 times for ASan per its documentation , 5 to 15 times for TSan per its documentation ), so they run in tests, not production.
On this Mac Apple's own ASan did not start (the root's Toolchain atlas records it); LLVM clang 23's worked, and every sanitizer report on this page is from it.

A hardened standard library : libc++ can check v[i] , front() , string_view bounds and more, turning silent UB into a trap ( libc++ hardening ). -D_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_FAST is meant for production (cheap checks, a silent trap); the _DEBUG mode prints why: index_oob.cpp #include <cstdio> #include <vector> int main() { std::vector< int > top{9491, 4816, 3499}; std::printf( "top[5] = %d\n" , top[5]); // [] does not check the index } $ clang++-23 -std=c++23 -O2 index_oob.cpp -o index_oob && ./index_oob top[5] = 69878144 $ clang++-23 -std=c++23 -O2 -D_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_DEBUG index_oob.cpp -o index_oob && ./index_oob vector.h:414: libc++ Hardening assertion __n < size() failed: vector[] index out of bounds (the shell reports: Abort trap: 6) [exit code 134] Initialise everything , or let the compiler do it: -ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero made the uninitialised example print "not seen" at -O2 .
C++26 makes this the language rule: reading an uninitialised local becomes erroneous behaviour , a defined (wrong) value the implementation may diagnose, instead of UB ( P2795 ).
Prefer what cannot be misused : .at(i) or a hardened library over raw indexing in non-hot code, smart pointers over new , values over references when lifetimes are unclear.
The honest summary No tool catches all UB, and sanitizers find only what your tests execute.
C++ makes you responsible for memory safety; Rust moves most of this list into compile errors (the root page's section 10, and the Rust page ).

The gates, with answers The questions that end each stage of the learning path (Reading 16 ).
Stage 0: what does the linker say when a non-inline function is defined in a header included from two .cpp files? "duplicate symbol" (ld on macOS; GNU ld says "multiple definition").
Each translation unit compiled its own copy, so two object files define the same symbol; the one definition rule allows only one.
Fix with inline , or keep only a declaration in the header.
The Build pipeline tab shows the real error.
Stage 1: when is each object in a function destroyed, and in what order?
Locals: at the closing brace of their block, in reverse order of construction; also during unwinding when an exception leaves the block.
Temporaries: at the end of the full expression (the semicolon), unless bound to a const& or && local, which extends them to that local's lifetime.
Members: after the class's destructor body, in reverse declaration order.
Heap objects: when their owner (a smart pointer) dies or is reset.
Stage 2: a class holds a unique_ptr and a vector .
Which special members does the compiler generate, which does it delete, and why?
It generates the destructor, the move constructor and the move assignment (member-wise; noexcept because both members' are).
It defines the copy constructor and copy assignment as deleted , because unique_ptr 's copy operations are deleted: a member-wise copy is impossible.
The class is move-only, like unique_ptr itself.
Declaring any of the five yourself would suppress the implicit moves, which is why the rule of zero says declare none.

Stage 3: why is std::vector<bool> a mistake, what does noexcept on a move constructor buy, and what may the optimiser assume about a signed loop counter? vector<bool> is specialised to pack bits, so it is not a container of bool : v[i] returns a proxy object, not a bool& , so bool& r = v[0] does not compile, &v[0] is not a bool* , and concurrent writes to different elements can race. noexcept lets vector move elements on reallocation instead of copying them (the Object lifetimes tab's two growth scenarios).
A signed counter never overflows, so i + 1 > i and the loop's trip count can be computed without wrap-around checks, which enables vectorisation and widening it to 64 bits.
Python hides the machine.
C++ hands it to you: the same loop can be 50 times faster or slower depending on where its data sits, how the compiler translated it and what other cores are doing.

Virtual memory, pages and mmap The addresses your program sees are not physical locations in the RAM chips.
They are virtual addresses : each process has its own private address space, and the operating system keeps a page table that maps it, one page at a time, to physical memory or to nothing yet.
On Apple silicon a page is 16 KB ( hw.pagesize printed 16384; Intel and most Linux machines use 4 KB).

Every load translates its address; the TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is the small cache of recent translations, and a miss in it costs extra loads to walk the page table, part of the slope you saw in the latency ladder.
Two consequences matter for C++ programmers: Memory is given lazily. malloc or new of a big block only reserves addresses.
The first touch of each page triggers a page fault : the processor stops, the kernel finds a physical page, zeroes it, maps it, and the instruction retries.

A file can be mapped instead of read. mmap puts a file's bytes into your address space; pages are read from disk (or from the operating system's page cache , the copy of recently used files it keeps in RAM) only when touched, and pages that are never touched cost nothing.
Filling fresh memory the first time took ms and the second time ms: the difference, spread over 16,384 page faults, is about microseconds per fault (three runs: ).

Mapping the 512 MB file took ms over three runs, whatever the file's size, and reading 8 bytes spread through it cost just 8 page faults; reading the whole file with read() took ms before the first byte was usable and doubled the memory in use.

Whether "touching every page" is fast depends on where the file is: in the page cache (minor faults, about 25 ms here) or only on the SSD (major faults: run 1 took about 0.9 s, because other programs had pushed the file out of RAM; its read() afterwards was fast because the mapping had just brought the file back into the page cache): Run 1 Run 2 Run 3 Why llama.cpp maps model files A model file is gigabytes of read-only weights.

Mapping it means loading is nearly instant, a second process running the same model shares the same physical pages through the page cache, a restart finds the weights still cached, and the operating system can drop pages under memory pressure and re-read them later instead of swapping.
The pinned llama.cpp source (commit 8e16421 ) does exactly this, with hints to the kernel about the access pattern: src/llama-mmap.cpp lines 482 to 498 .
Part 3 follows the loader that calls it.

In Python numpy.memmap , safetensors ' lazy loading and torch.load(..., mmap=True) are the same system call. "The model loaded instantly but the first token was slow" is page faults being paid on first use.
The compiler's view: reading assembly A compiler (here clang, which hands its work to LLVM) translates C++ into machine code , the instructions the processor runs.
Assembly is the readable text form of machine code.
You do not need to write it; reading a little of it is the only reliable way to know what your C++ became.
Get it with clang++ -O2 -S file.cpp -o - , or paste code into Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) , which colours each source line and its instructions alike.

It needs the function's body to be visible: in the same file, in a header, or with link-time optimisation ( -flto ).

SIMD: one instruction, several numbers SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) instructions apply one operation to a short vector of values held in one wide register.
On ARM the SIMD instruction set is NEON : 32 registers of 128 bits, each holding 4 floats, 8 16-bit values or 16 bytes. fmla v0.4s, v1.4s, v2.4s does four multiply-adds at once.
On x86, the same ideas are SSE (128 bits), AVX2 (256 bits: 8 floats) and AVX-512 (512 bits: 16 floats), with intrinsics such as _mm256_fmadd_ps ( Intel intrinsics guide ).

This M1 Pro also reports the dot-product extension for 8-bit integers ( FEAT_DotProd : 1), but not BF16, I8MM or SME (all 0 in the sysctl output above); llama.cpp's quantised kernels check for exactly these features.

There are three ways to get SIMD code: let the compiler vectorise a plain loop, write intrinsics (C functions that map one to one onto SIMD instructions, from <arm_neon.h> ; Arm intrinsics reference ), or call a library that did (BLAS, Accelerate, ggml).
Here is a dot product, the core operation of every matrix product, written three ways and compiled a fourth way: Predict.
On two vectors of 4096 floats (32 KB in all, inside L1), how much faster than the scalar loop is the plain loop at -O2 ?
And the NEON version?

From DRAM every version that is fast enough hits the same wall, about 56 GB/s for one core ( section 9 ).

Why: dependency chains, not instruction counts Switch between the four loops' assembly (the inner loop is the block that ends with b.ne back to its label): Scalar : one fmadd per element, each adding into s0 , so each must wait for the previous one: 4 cycles each (the latency of fmadd on this core).">scalar -O2 : 16 elements per iteration, multiplied 4 at a time ( fmul.4s ), but then the 16 products are added into s0 one by one, in source order (16 fadd s in a chain, 3 cycles each).
Only the multiplications were vectorised.">-O2 -O2 -ffast-math : four vector accumulators v0 .. v3 , each a chain of fmla.4s : 16 running sums, combined at the end with fadd.4s and faddp .

Allowed only because fast-math permits reordering additions.">-ffast-math NEON intrinsics : the same 4 x fmla.4s loop as fast-math, written by hand, without changing the rounding rules for the whole file.">intrinsics A small model predicts the measured times from two published latencies, 4 cycles for a fused multiply-add and 3 for an add on this core ( Dougall Johnson's Firestorm tables ), and a clock of 3.2 GHz (inferred: the add chain's measured ns per element divided into 3 cycles gives GHz): The time is set by the longest chain of instructions that wait for each other, not by how many instructions there are.
Independent accumulators break the chain; SIMD lanes multiply the work per instruction.
The SIMD lanes tab animates the three schedules on the same 16 numbers.

Fast-math changed the answer On the 67-million-element vectors the results differ: the serial loops printed , the 16-accumulator loops ; the exact sum (computed in Python with exact arithmetic on the same inputs) is .
The serial float sum is 23% low: once the running total is large, adding a small product to it rounds away most of the product.
Sixteen partial sums stay smaller and lose less.

So reordering is not "less accurate" in general: it is different , and here better. -ffast-math also assumes there are no NaNs or infinities, which can silently break code that checks for them; prefer intrinsics, a local permission such as clang's #pragma clang fp reassociate(on) at the top of one function (checked here: the plain loop then compiles to fmla.4s accumulators, src/cb/code/reassoc.cpp ), or a library.

The same loop in llama.cpp ggml's float dot product is this exact design: on NEON, GGML_F32_STEP 16 floats per iteration as 4 registers of GGML_F32_EPR 4 lanes, each with its own accumulator. ggml-cpu/simd-mappings.h L331-345 ggml-cpu/vec.cpp L104-126 In NumPy np.dot on float32 calls a BLAS library that does all of this (and on macOS, Accelerate may use Apple's matrix hardware). sum() in pure Python on floats is the serial chain, plus the interpreter; math.fsum trades speed for an exactly rounded result.
Branch prediction A modern core works on hundreds of instructions at once, in a pipeline : fetching and decoding later instructions while earlier ones finish.
At an if it cannot wait to learn which way to go, so a branch predictor guesses from the branch's history and the core runs ahead on the guess.
A right guess is free.
A wrong one (a misprediction ) throws away the work done on the wrong path and restarts.
Random data makes guessing impossible; sorted data makes it trivial.
The test counts and sums the bytes that are at least 128 in 32 million random bytes, then the same bytes sorted: Predict.
Compiled normally at -O2 : how much faster is the sorted run?
Reveal the real output -O2 No difference, and both very fast: the compiler removed the branch.
It turned if (v[i] >= 128) s += v[i] into SIMD code that compares 16 bytes at once and adds them through a mask, so there is nothing left to predict.
The famous result (a Stack Overflow question with tens of thousands of votes) only appears when the branch stays.

Built with -DKEEP_BRANCH , which puts an empty asm volatile("") inside the if so the compiler must keep a real branch ( tbz , "test bit and branch if zero", on the byte's top bit): -O2, branch kept Unsorted, half the branches go each way at random and the predictor is wrong about half the time; sorted, it is almost never wrong.
The cost of one misprediction, derived: ( - ) ns / 0.5 mispredictions per element = ns, about cycles at 3.2 GHz (an upper estimate: it includes the loop's other work that the wrong path delayed).

What to do: in hot loops over data you cannot sort, prefer branch-free forms (a conditional select, s += v[i] >= 128 ? v[i] : 0 , which compiles to csel or a SIMD mask), and check in the assembly that the compiler did it.
Do not reach for [[likely]] and [[unlikely]] to fix this: they change code layout, not the predictor's hit rate.
In NumPy a[a >= 128].sum() and np.where are branch-free by construction: they compute a mask for the whole array and then apply it.
That is the vectorised style the compiler found here.

The roofline: compute-bound or memory-bound?
Every kernel needs two resources: arithmetic and bytes from memory.
The roofline model ( Williams, Waterman and Patterson, 2009 ) asks which one runs out first.
Define the kernel's arithmetic intensity I as floating-point operations per byte moved from memory.

Then attainable FLOP/s = min( peak FLOP/s , I × bandwidth ) I FLOPs per byte read from DRAM (a multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs) peak the core's or chip's maximum arithmetic rate bandwidth bytes per second the memory system delivers Below the ridge point I = peak / bandwidth, a kernel is memory-bound : a faster processor would not help, only fewer bytes would.
Above it, it is compute-bound .

The inputs, measured here ( roof.cpp , compiled with -O3 -ffast-math ; three runs each): The peak loop runs 24 independent fmla.4s chains so that all four floating-point units stay busy (4 units x 4 lanes x 2 FLOPs = 32 FLOPs per cycle, about 102 GFLOP/s at 3.2 GHz; measured ).
A first version with 12 chains of the form a = y + a * x reached only 64 GFLOP/s: the compiler had to add a register copy before every fmla , because fmla overwrites its accumulator.
The bandwidth row is reading a 512 MB array once: one core reaches about half of the chip's 200 GB/s, all eight about GB/s (the GPU shares the rest).
The matrix-vector product is LLM decoding.
Generating one token multiplies every weight matrix by one vector: each weight is read once and used for one multiply-add.
In fp32 that is 2 FLOPs per 4 bytes, I = 0.5, far left of the ridge: the bound is 0.5 x bandwidth, and the measured matvec sits right on it.
So decoding speed is set by bytes: tokens per second can be at most bandwidth / bytes of weights.

Illustrative (not measured): an 8-billion-parameter model in 16-bit weights is 16 GB, so at GB/s this laptop could produce at most about tokens per second however fast its arithmetic; in llama.cpp's 4-bit q4_0 format (18 bytes per 32 weights, 4.5 bits each) it is 4.5 GB and the ceiling rises to about .

This is why quantisation speeds up decoding and why batching many users' tokens together (which reuses each weight for many vectors, raising I) is the core of LLM serving; both belong to Topic: inference-and-serving and the Quantization and Precision page.

The matrix-matrix product is compute-bound (I about 85 FLOPs per byte for 512 x 512 matrices read once), yet the simple tiled loop reached only about a quarter of peak: it is limited by loads and stores inside the core, not by DRAM.
Libraries close that gap with register blocking (keeping a small tile of the output in registers across the whole inner loop); that craft is the subject of Topic: cuda-and-gpu-programming on the GPU.
The Roofline tab plots these points and lets you move a batch-size slider to see decode cross the ridge.

Allocation: the hidden cost Every new or make_unique calls the allocator ( malloc ), which must find free space, record it, and later free it; and each object lands somewhere else on the heap, so a container of pointers is a pointer chase (section 1).
A growing std::vector reallocates when full, copying or moving every element into a buffer about twice as big.

Ten million separate heap objects cost about x as much as one reserved vector (three runs: ms against ms); growth without reserve moved the buffer 25 times but cost little, because doubling makes the total copying about twice the final size.
The last lines show the small-string optimisation : a std::string object here is 24 bytes, and strings of up to 22 characters live inside it with no heap allocation at all.

Rules: reserve when you know the size, store values rather than pointers, reuse buffers across iterations, and make large objects movable so that containers move rather than copy them ( Part 1 covers move semantics).

The ABI: C++'s binary contract An API is a contract in source code: names, types, what functions do.

An ABI (application binary interface) is the contract between already-compiled pieces of machine code: which registers carry arguments (section 5), how structs are laid out (section 3), how virtual tables and exceptions work, and what the symbols are called.
Two object files work together only if they agree on all of it.
Python programmers meet the ABI as "this wheel does not match your Python" or as a crash after mixing builds.
Name mangling C has one function per name.

C++ allows the same name in different namespaces and overloads with different parameter types, so the compiler encodes the namespace and the parameter types into the symbol, following the Itanium C++ ABI (used by clang and GCC on every platform except Windows, despite its name). extern "C" turns mangling off, which is why every C++ library meant to be called from another language exposes a C interface.
Read __ZN9ggml_like3dotEPKfS1_i as: _Z a mangled name (macOS adds one more underscore in front), N ...
E a nested name made of 9ggml_like (9 characters) and 3dot , then the parameters: PKf pointer to const float, S1_ the same type again, i int.
The double overload differs only in d . c_dot is just _c_dot .
What breaks when you mix Different standard libraries. clang on macOS uses libc++; GCC on Linux uses libstdc++.
Their std::string , std::vector and friends have different layouts, so a std::string cannot cross between code built against the two.
Even within one library, flags that change layouts (debug iterators, _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI on Linux) must match.
Standard library designs that cannot be fixed.

Because programs compiled years ago still link against today's shared standard library, library vendors avoid any change to a type's layout or a function's mangled name; known-slow designs ( std::unordered_map 's node-based buckets, std::regex ) stay as they are for that reason.
Headers and flags out of step.
Two translation units that see different definitions of the same struct (a different #define , packing pragma or alignment) break the one-definition rule: no error, just corrupted fields at run time.

Mixing compilers is fine through a C interface, risky through C++ types, and the reason C++ has no universal package of prebuilt binaries like PyPI's wheels ( Part 1 covers builds and package managers).
Apple's ARM64 ABI differs from the standard Linux one in a few details (for example, how variadic arguments are passed): Writing ARM64 code for Apple platforms .

In Python ctypes and cffi can call only C symbols, so they need extern "C" . pybind11 and nanobind compile C++ against CPython's own C ABI; a wheel built for one Python version works only on that version unless it uses the limited "abi3" stable ABI (the Rust page covers abi3 wheels with PyO3).
To the GPU: what changes Everything above carries over to GPUs, with the dials turned.

GGUF: the model file A model file must carry the weights and everything needed to use them: architecture, sizes, tokenizer, chat template.
GGUF is llama.cpp's format for that: one file, read without Python and without parsing JSON.
The format is written down at the top of gguf.h : Every integer has a fixed width and is little-endian; a string is a 64-bit length then the bytes.
That is what makes it easy to read from any language.
Here is a complete reader in 41 lines of Python, standard library only, run on our model file: The file to scale.
The header is bytes, mostly the tokenizer's 49,152 token strings and 48,900 merge rules; then padding to a multiple of 32; then tensors back to back.
Three details to notice.
Shapes are stored innermost first: token_embd.weight has ne=[576, 49152] , where PyTorch would say (49152, 576) ; ne[0] is the dimension whose elements are adjacent in memory.
Offsets are relative to the start of the data section, which begins at byte , the end of the header rounded up to the alignment of 32 (so every tensor can be loaded with aligned SIMD reads, Part 2).
Sizes follow from the type: Q8_0 stores 32 weights in 34 bytes, so the embedding table is 576 × 49,152 / 32 × 34 = bytes.

The C++ reader computes the byte strides from the same numbers: The project's own Python package, gguf-py (used by the converters that turn Hugging Face checkpoints into GGUF), reads the same thing and adds names for the types: C++ in gguf.cpp The reader is C++ behind a C API: a gguf_reader struct with overloaded read() functions for each type (templates, Part 1 section 8 ), std::vector and std::string for the values, and try / catch (std::bad_alloc &) around reads whose length comes from the file, because a corrupt or malicious file can claim a string of 2 63 bytes.
Every count is checked against SIZE_MAX before allocating: reading untrusted binary input is where C and C++ code gets exploited (Part 1, UB gallery ).
The model has 134.5 million parameters stored mostly as Q8_0.
Before looking: is the file bigger or smaller than 134.5 million bytes, and by roughly how much?
Reveal the real answer Bigger: bytes.
Q8_0 spends 34 bytes on 32 weights (8.5 bits each, the scale costs the extra half bit), 61 small norm vectors stay in 32-bit float, and the header adds 1.8 MB.
The loader reports 8.51 BPW (bits per weight).

text: The CPU backend: threads, barriers, chunks The CPU backend runs the graph with a pool of threads (4 by default, GGML_DEFAULT_N_THREADS ).

section: 9. the cpu backend: threads, barriers, chunks

KV cache, batches and sampling What the KV cache is and why it exists is Topic: inference-and-serving 's subject.

In the code it is a class with virtual functions, implementing an abstract interface (C++ inheritance, Part 1 section 7 ): llama_memory_i has several implementations (a plain cache, one with a sliding window, one for recurrent models), and the context holds whichever the model needs through a pointer to the interface.
Storage is one K tensor and one V tensor per layer.

Writing this token's K is a SET_ROWS node: copy rows into the cache at the slot indices chosen for this batch: Reading K for attention is a 4-dimensional view of the same tensor: no copy, just sizes and strides (section 6).
The view in our trace was {64, 3, 256} : 64 numbers per head, 3 KV heads, 256 cells.

Size, from the log: KV buffer size = MiB = 2 (K and V) × 30 layers × cells × 192 numbers × 2 bytes (F16) = bytes. simple.cpp asked for a context of 12 tokens (prompt + 8 − 1); the context rounds it up to cells ( cparams.n_ctx = GGML_PAD(cparams.n_ctx, 256); in llama-context.cpp ).

A batch is a list of tokens, each with a position, a sequence id (which conversation it belongs to) and a flag saying whether its logits are wanted. simple.cpp fills one with the prompt and asks for logits only for the last token, which is what lets the graph drop the other rows before the output projection: Sampling.
Samplers are written in the C style: an interface is a struct of function pointers, and each sampler fills one in.

The interface, and greedy sampling, which takes the token with the highest logit: So the same codebase writes interfaces two ways: the KV cache as a C++ class with virtual functions, the samplers and the backends as C structs of function pointers, because they are part of the C API that other languages call.
The program in section 7 does both side by side and prints the same token.
The server llama-server (in tools/server/ , 20,000 lines of C++) serves the model over HTTP with an OpenAI-compatible API.

Its central idea: several requests share one context, each in a slot , and every step puts the next token of every active slot into one batch (continuous batching; the idea and its trade-offs are Topic: inference-and-serving 's).

A slot is a C++ struct with owning smart pointers: The step loop calls the same llama_process as simple.cpp , inside a lambda that captures everything by reference ( [&] ), handed to the task queue so that metrics requests can be answered while the model runs ( Part 1 section 10, Lambdas ): A real request to the server started with 2 slots ( -np 2 ) on the CPU: The same 8 tokens as simple.cpp , about ms each instead of : the server adds HTTP, JSON, a task queue and per-token work for streaming and stop strings, and ran on the same busy laptop.
A Python service calling it (or the Node and Rust clients on the sibling pages) only sees the JSON.

From Python This is the role vLLM or Text Generation Inference play in Python land: a scheduler that batches requests around one model. llama-server is the C++ version for a single machine, often a laptop.
